item.research_question: How do the synthesis methods and operating temperatures influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and tribological performance (friction and wear) of high-entropy coatings (HECs) in various industrial applications?
item.material_system: High-entropy coatings (HECs) including metallic (e.g., CuMoTaWV, FeCoCrNiMo0.2, AlCrTiV), ceramic (e.g., (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N, TiVCrZrWNx), and composite systems; base elements include Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Al, Ti, V, Mo, W, Ta, Nb, Zr, Si, Cu, Mn.
item.processing_route: Fabrication via vapor deposition (magnetron sputtering, reactive sputtering, vacuum arc), thermal spraying (atmospheric plasma spray (APS), high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF)), and cladding (laser, plasma). Key parameters include substrate bias voltage (0 to -200 V), nitrogen flow rate (FN), substrate temperature (300 °C), annealing (300 °C), and feedstock preparation (mechanical alloying, gas atomization).
item.test_conditions: Tribological testing performed using ball-on-disk and pin-on-disk setups against counterfaces of Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15). Tests conducted from room temperature (RT) up to 600 °C, varying sliding speeds, loads, and sliding distances.
key_findings: The CuMoTaWV coating exhibited adaptive tribological behavior: lowest coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rate at RT due to Ta- and W-rich tribo-layers; galling wear at 200 °C; reduced wear at 400 °C due to adaptive CuO formation; and low COF but slightly higher wear at 600 °C due to excessive V-rich phase oxidation.

In (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N coatings, increasing substrate bias from 0 V to -200 V increased hardness from 28.2 GPa to 34.5 GPa and reduced wear rate to 1.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m at -100 V, attributed to grain boundary strengthening and denser structure.
The (AlCrTiVZr)N film deposited at a nitrogen flow of 12 sccm achieved super-hardness of 41.8 GPa and a low wear rate of 2.3 × 10−7 mm3/N.m.
The FeCoCrNiMo0.2 coating fabricated via APS showed a volume wear rate of 3.9 × 10−5 mm3/N.m, significantly lower than the HVOF coating (4.8 × 10−4 mm3/N.m) and the substrate (5.4 × 10−4 mm3/N.m).
TiVCrZrWNx coatings formed a self-lubricating V2O5 phase during rolling friction, reducing the friction coefficient to 0.38.
The (CrNbSiTiZr)C film exhibited a minimum friction coefficient of 0.3 and a wear rate of 4.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m due to the formation of a transfer film and high H/E (0.151) and H3/E2 (0.747) ratios.
Annealing the CuMoTaWV film at 300 °C improved its adhesion and wear resistance at both room temperature and 300 °C compared to the as-deposited state.
item.mechanism: Tribological improvements are attributed to the formation of self-lubricating oxide layers (e.g., CuO, MoO3, V2O5) at elevated temperatures, the high hardness and nano-crystalline grain structure of the coatings, the presence of secondary phases (e.g., V-rich zones), and the balance between hardness and toughness enhanced by substrate bias or plasma nitriding. Wear mechanisms vary from adhesive wear and galling at intermediate temperatures to mild abrasive wear and oxidative wear at higher temperatures.
item.limitations: The text notes that results from different wear experiments using different tools and parameters may not be directly comparable. It also highlights that there is very limited information available regarding high-entropy coatings developed by vapor deposition and cold spray methods compared to thermal spraying and cladding.
item.future_work: The authors state that further investigation is needed to optimize process parameters, explore more manufacturing processes (especially for HEA wires and targets), and conduct more extensive and interdisciplinary tribological investigations at high temperatures to better understand the complex wear-related phenomena.
quotes: At RT, the lowest COF and wear rate was observed due to the formation of the Ta- and W-rich tribo layer in the wear track.

The promotion of mechanical performance was ascribed to the strengthening effects of coatings, including grain boundary strengthening, denser structure, and more ion-induced defects, when substrate bias was applied.
The volume wear rate of the APS coating was about 3.9 × 10−5 mm3/N.m, which was significantly lower than the HVOF coating (4.8 × 10−4 mm3/N.m) and the substrate (5.4 × 10−4 mm3/N.m).

item.research_question: How does the addition of Silver (Ag) and the variation in temperature affect the tribological properties and wear mechanisms of plasma-sprayed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-based high-entropy coatings?
item.material_system: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-Ag (HEA-Ag) and Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti (HEC) coatings formed on carbon steel
item.test_conditions: Temperature range from 25 to 750 °C; ball-on-disk sliding; counterface not explicitly named in the specific Li et al. summary but implied standard tribological testing
key_findings: At high temperatures (600–750 °C), the HEA-Ag coating achieved a friction coefficient of 0.253 and a wear rate of 0.89 × 10−5 mm3/N.m at 750 °C.
The wear rate of both HEA and HEA + Ag coatings was significantly lower than that of tool steels SKH 51 and Q 125 at all test temperatures.
At low temperatures (RT to 400 °C), tribological properties depended on mechanical properties and Ag lubrication.
The addition of Ag had little effect on the friction coefficient at high temperatures.
The as-sprayed coatings comprised a major FCC solid solution with minor BCC phase.
A lubricious film consisting of Ag and various oxides formed on the frictional surface.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the outstanding tribological properties at high temperatures to the formation of a lubricious film on the frictional surface consisting of Ag and various oxides, which contributes to low friction and wear. At low temperatures, the properties are governed by the mechanical properties of the coating and the solid lubrication provided by Ag.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations for this specific study, only that the study investigated the effect of Ag addition and temperature.
quotes: a relatively low friction coefficient (0.253) and wear rate (0.89 × 10−5 mm3/N.m) was achieved at 750 °C for HEA-Ag coating
The authors reported that the lubricious film that was formed consisted of Ag and various oxides on the frictional surface
The wear rate of both HEA and HEA + Ag was significantly lower than that of tool steels SKH 51 and Q 125 at all the test temperatures
